items.ig_caption:
Plasma freezers. Someone tried to set them to 110°C. Remotely. 🧊

What SecurityWeek / AP reported (5 Nov):
→ France's blood service EFS says temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels at three plasma cold-storage sites on Monday
→ The attack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment; per Le Canard Enchaîné it tried to reset -30°C storage to as high as 110°C
→ Monitoring systems quickly detected it; plasma was transferred or secured
→ EFS: "no blood products or samples were compromised" and collection continues
→ Supplier Coolworld says the flaw is in a third-party component and few units were affected; France's cyber agency is investigating

What to do: list every vendor that can change setpoints on your cooling or OT systems remotely, put alarms on out-of-range changes, and make sure someone gets paged.

cover.hook: A certificate authority's VPN-only system ended up on the internet. For over a year.
cover.sub: DigiCert says an unauthorized account read archived customer data, including some ID documents.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: Per DigiCert's incident report, a February 2025 server migration exposed an internal business system that used to be reachable only over VPN. A self-registration feature plus an authorization flaw let new accounts read archived customer data.

slides.label: from finding rogue accounts (June) to confirming data access (19 Oct)
slides.note: Access happened 27 Jun to 2 Jul 2026, per BleepingComputer

slides.title: What was exposed
slides.body: Names, business emails, phone numbers and business addresses. For some people: an ID document such as a driver's licence, passport or utility bill. DigiCert is still reviewing which ID documents were involved.

slides.title: What DigiCert says wasn't
slides.body: The account was read-only and could not issue certificates or approve validations. CertCentral and DigiCert ONE were not compromised, and "customer login credentials and issued certificates remain secure."

slides.title: Do this week
items: Re-test every system after a migration: is it still VPN-only?
Turn off self-registration you don't need
Treat odd new accounts as a possible data-access event
Watch for phishing that uses your DigiCert details

items.question: After your last server migration, did anyone check what became reachable from the internet?
items.x_text:
DigiCert data breach: a 2025 server migration exposed a VPN-only internal system; an unauthorized account read archived customer data, including some ID documents, 27 Jun-2 Jul 2026. DigiCert says certificates and logins are secure.

items.ig_caption:
A certificate authority's VPN-only system ended up on the internet. 🔓

What BleepingComputer reported (5 Nov):
→ DigiCert says a February 2025 server migration exposed an internal business system that was previously reachable only via VPN
→ A self-registration feature plus an authorization flaw let new accounts read archived customer data
→ An unauthorized account accessed it between 27 Jun and 2 Jul 2026; DigiCert first treated it as "an account-creation issue rather than a data-access event" and confirmed access on 19 Oct
→ Exposed: names, business emails, phone numbers, business addresses and, for some, an ID document like a passport or driver's licence
→ DigiCert says the account couldn't issue certificates, and CertCentral and DigiCert ONE were not compromised

What to do: re-check exposure after every migration, disable self-registration you don't need, and treat strange new accounts as a possible data-access event.

cover.hook: Free ChatGPT Pro. Just sign in with your work account.
cover.sub: Fake OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic event pages are stealing Microsoft and Google sessions, Push Security says.

slides.title: The lure
slides.body: Fake event pages promise "free access to premium AI services": three months of ChatGPT Pro at an OpenAI marketing event, Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share" at a SpaceX event. A fake Anthropic AWS re:Invent page was already taken down.

slides.title: The Microsoft path
slides.body: "Continue with Microsoft" generates a device code. The victim types it on Microsoft's real login page, which hands the attacker tokens for their Entra account. A second page can also grab the password and session cookie.

slides.label: phishing-as-a-service platforms: Kali365 and VoidProxy
slides.note: Per Push Security, via BleepingComputer, 5 Nov 2026

slides.title: The Google path
slides.body: "Continue with Google" opens a VoidProxy pop-up that proxies the real login and steals credentials, MFA responses and session cookies. Links pass through Google and Zapier shorteners, with a Cloudflare CAPTCHA to block scanners.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Restrict device code sign-in where it isn't needed
Move admins to phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 keys)
Tell staff: never type a device code a website gives you
Flag event invites that need a work sign-in for rewards

items.question: Does your organisation still allow device code sign-in for everyone?

#Phishing #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Free ChatGPT Pro. Just sign in with your work account. 🎣

What BleepingComputer reported (5 Nov), from Push Security research:
→ Fake OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic event pages offer free AI perks like three months of ChatGPT Pro or Grok Heavy
→ "Continue with Microsoft" triggers device code phishing (Kali365): the victim enters a code on Microsoft's real site and the attacker gets tokens
→ "Continue with Google" opens a VoidProxy page that steals credentials, MFA responses and session cookies
→ Links run through Google and Zapier shorteners, behind a Cloudflare CAPTCHA to dodge scanners
→ Push Security saw and blocked visits in late October

What to do: restrict device code authentication where it isn't needed, use phishing-resistant MFA like FIDO2 keys, and tell staff never to enter a device code a website hands them.

→ Fixed on 28 Oct in WordPress 7.1.4, with backports to branches through 4.7
→ Wordfence's first firewall match came nine minutes after deployment; 18,500+ requests in the first 21 hours
→ Wordfence has not reported successful compromises
→ CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 3 Nov

What to do: confirm every site is on 7.1.4 or its branch's backported release, and don't wait for auto-updates on sites where they're off.
